li.a: Herald Business: PPP lawmaker introduces bill to investigate mass killings at Seoul National University Hospital during Korean War
Herald Kyungje: Yu Yong-won sponsors special bill on the Seoul National University Hospital massacre during the 1950 war (in Korean)
a Korean medical newspaper: 76 years since the Seoul National University Hospital massacre, the devotion of medical staff (in Korean)
Yonhap News: Remember the unnamed soldiers who resisted the 1950 killings of wounded soldiers and medical staff (in Korean)
Opinion column, 2024: The bare face of Korea in crisis
PubMed Central: The causes and numbers of hospital admissions and deaths during the Korean War (2024)

content.p: In the last days of June 1950, the Korean War was barely three days old when North Korean troops were, by one 2024 newspaper column's account, closing in on the gate of Seoul National University Hospital. The building, in Yeongeon-dong in the Jongno district of the capital, had filled with South Korean soldiers wounded in the fighting to the north. According to a 2025 report by South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, North Korean troops entered the hospital on 28 June 1950 and, in two incidents on 28 and 29 June, killed wounded soldiers and civilian patients. More than seven decades later, the sources still disagree about how many people died.
content.h2: A hospital that was already full
content.p: The war began in the early hours of 25 June 1950, when North Korean forces began shelling across the 38th parallel and then advanced with heavily armed infantry supported by armour. A 2024 study of South Korean military hospital records, drawing on a confidential 1955 army history, counted 397,519 admissions during the whole war, with 53.9 per cent of admissions listed as wounded in action.

Yu Yong-won, a People Power Party lawmaker, whose office cites historical records and testimony, says that large numbers of South Korean wounded soldiers had been evacuated to the hospital from fighting around Uijeongbu and along the Miari Pass defensive line. A nursing assistant who was present gave testimony, cited by Yu's office, that wounded soldiers began arriving in large numbers on 26 June. By 27 June all 800 beds were occupied, and patients lay in the emergency room, the operating theatres and the corridors. The estimated number of patients admitted over the period exceeded 1,000.

Yu's office and the records it cites put the first attack at about 9 a.m. on 28 June. A South Korean Army guard platoon was defending the hospital. Yonhap and a Korean medical newspaper identify the unit as a platoon from the Army Headquarters Logistics School, led by a major and a second lieutenant, and say that it stayed behind to protect the medical staff and the wounded. Both outlets report that the platoon fought until it was wiped out.

After the platoon was destroyed, the North Korean troops held the building. Yu's office says they shot the wounded soldiers and civilian patients inside, without distinction. The Herald Business report adds, citing accounts that it says have emerged, that medical staff were forcibly taken into the North Korean military and that most were taken north. The report does not name those accounts, so the claim is given here as an allegation.

The Korean coverage includes the memory of a witness who was 95 years old at the 2026 memorial service. He had been a student at a school near the hospital in 1950. Speaking to a Yonhap reporter there, he recalled that the street outside was full of bodies. a Korean medical newspaper reported the same account. It is one man's recollection of a scene near the hospital, and it does not give a count.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's 2025 finding, as quoted in a Korean report, describes two separate killings: the first on 28 June and the second on 29 June. The commission concluded that North Korean forces had entered the hospital in the morning of 28 June and unlawfully killed the South Korean soldiers and civilian patients who were being treated there. A Korean medical newspaper and Yonhap describe the event mainly as a single attack on 28 June, so the two-day sequence is the commission's version and not one all the sources repeat.

A 2024 opinion column about the doctors' protest over medical school places described the same hospital in shorter terms. It said that North Korean soldiers barged in and fired on the bedridden patients and the medical staff who had stayed with them, and that survivors were shot or taken hostage. The column gives no source for those details, and its author was writing about a different subject, so this report treats it as a commentator's summary rather than an account of the events.

The figures in the sources differ, and each comes from a different maker. Before the commission reported, estimates based on the number of patients, the size of the wards and witness accounts ran from 900 to about 1,000 or more, according to a Korean medical newspaper and Yonhap. The Herald Business report, citing Yu's office and the historical records compiled so far, describes approximately 1,000 wounded soldiers and civilian patients massacred. The opinion column gives a figure of around 900 killed on the premises.

The commission's own finding is narrower. It estimated the total number of victims at about 1,000, but said that about 330 of them had been confirmed through its investigation. Yonhap and a Korean medical newspaper both report the 330 figure, and both make clear that it is a confirmed count, not a total. The sources do not explain the gap between the 330 confirmed and the 1,000 estimated.

Yu's bill itself says that the number of victims has not been officially confirmed, and it sets out a committee that would study that question. Until the committee reports, the number should be read as an estimate, with the source named each time it is used.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, in its second term, issued its report on the hospital in 2025. Yonhap reports that the commission decided in April 2025 that the killings were established as truth, and that it recommended steps for the government. These included urging the North Korean government to apologise, excavating a suspected burial site linked to the hospital, restoring the honour of the victims and their families, and supporting memorial work.

The report named the perpetrators in the way its investigation could support. According to the Herald Business summary, it identified about 50 soldiers from North Korea's 4th Division and nine Workers' Party members from the Seongdong district of Seoul, whose names are unknown. It asked the state to treat the mass shooting of wounded soldiers and civilian patients as a breach of the Geneva Conventions and a clear-cut war crime. Those findings belong to the commission and are given as its findings, not as established facts about every individual.
content.h2: A bill, a memorial and an anniversary
content.p: On 24 June 2026, Yu introduced the special bill. It would create a committee under the prime minister to investigate the true facts of the incident, including the victims not yet officially confirmed, and to restore the honour of the dead and their families. The committee would have three years to gather and analyse the material, and it would then have six months to submit a final report to the National Assembly. The bill would also allow the national and local governments to pay for a memorial tower, a memorial park, an archive and human rights and security education. Herald Business quotes Yu as saying that "a full accounting of the circumstances of the massacre and the exact number of victims has not been achieved", and that the legal and institutional basis for restoring the victims' honour had yet to be put in place.

The memorial in front of the hospital is a monument to the unnamed fighters who died there. A Korean medical newspaper reports that a state ministry designated it a state memorial facility in March 2026. The hospital has held a memorial service there every year since 2014. The 2026 service, held on 26 June, was attended by the hospital's director, the head of the Seoul North regional office of the state veterans ministry, and the heads of nine veterans' organisations in Jongno district, according to Yonhap. The hospital's director also praised the staff who kept carrying and treating the wounded, according to a Korean medical newspaper.
content.h2: Points the sources do not settle
content.p: The first is the death toll. The commission's 330 confirmed victims and its roughly 1,000 estimate, the pre-report estimates of 900 to 1,000, the JoongAng column's 900 and the Herald's figure of about 1,000 are all in circulation, and they are not reconciled in any of the sources.

The second is the timing. The commission describes two incidents, on 28 and 29 June. a Korean medical newspaper and Yonhap describe the killings on 28 June. Yu's office gives both dates. The reader should treat the 29 June attack as the commission's finding rather than a fact every source confirms.

The third is the fate of the medical staff. The Herald Business report says most were taken to the North, citing accounts it did not name. A report in Korean on Yu's release says the same, that they were reported to have been taken north, without naming a source. The commission's findings as reported do not mention the claim. It is an allegation that remains open.

The fourth is the identity of the attackers. The commission named units and a district but no individuals, and it said their names were unknown. An account that names a person as responsible would need a source, and none of the sources listed gives one.
